# Part of the research family

## Authors

- Emma Pewsey<sup>1</sup> ([ORCID: 0000-0002-2475-7775](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-2475-7775)) †

### Affiliations

1. Features eLife Cambridge United Kingdom

† Corresponding author

## Abstract

eLife is publishing a collection of articles and interviews with scientists who are parents to explore how to get the best of both worlds.

## Where’s the childcare?

Some of the problems faced by scientists who are parents will be familiar to parents of all professions. A key pressure point is the cost and availability of childcare, and many researchers would like on-campus childcare to be provided. However, even researchers fortunate enough to work for an institute that provides childcare facilities face barriers to using them. On-campus nurseries often have months-long waiting lists, making early registration essential. “I know of a couple who booked their child in before the baby was even conceived”, says Marta Garrido of the University of Queensland. Marta herself had to wait two years for a full-time place for her first son, having registered him six months before he was born.

The costs of the facilities can also be prohibitive, particularly for early-career researchers. And even with subsidies, the cost of full-time care for one child often represents over half of a researcher’s salary. That’s when they’re able to use the facilities at all: postdoctoral researchers paid through scholarships may not be officially employed by the institution they work at, and so are ineligible for on-site nurseries provided for the children of staff and students. This situation is one example of the wider disparities in the benefits on offer to different classes of postdoctoral researchers, which have led to calls for the employment contracts of postdocs to be made more consistent (Schaller et al., 2017).

## Time out

The parental leave on offer to researchers varies widely. National standards and the gender of the parent are the main factor controlling the length of leave available, although the situation is more complicated for graduate students and postdocs on fixed-term contracts. Furthermore, parents on short-term contracts that come to an end around the time of birth can find themselves unemployed instead of on leave. Even without these pressures, researchers may choose to work through their leave period: papers and funding applications need to be written, and junior lab members need mentoring. Although the collaborative nature of science means that others may be able to help with some tasks, it can also make parents feel like they’re taking advantage of their colleagues if they take leave.

A number of initiatives offered by employers, funders and other organizations aim to provide parents with more time for research once they return from maternity leave. For example, Gaby Da Silva Xavier of Imperial College used an Elsie Widdowson Fellowship from the university to employ a technician to help run her lab.

![Figure](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/36707/elife-36707-fig1-v1.jpg)

## Travelling the distance

The perceived career benefits of mobility – particularly for early-career researchers – means that many scientists will bring up their children in a foreign country. In addition, short-term contracts can cause researchers to move their family repeatedly, leaving them far from their support networks.

In the course of this series we will feature several stories of researchers living or working in a different country to their children or partner for months at a time. Ali Twelvetrees, for example, had her child in Philadelphia in 2015, and moved to London in 2016 to complete her Fellowship; meanwhile her postdoc husband Dan remained in Philadelphia for another year to complete his project. “Emotionally and financially it was very hard”, says Ali. “I love being a mum, but not being able to share childcare with anyone in that period made the daily grind relentless”. Ali and Dan now have their own labs at the University of Sheffield.

Even when researchers can avoid emigrating, travelling for conferences and meetings still presents difficulties. Although some conference organizers are starting to offer funding and meeting rooms to help with childcare, many researchers are still faced with a difficult choice between spending time away from their children or losing out on networking opportunities. “I feel bad leaving my daughter alone with my husband for too long, but at the same time I feel bad rejecting invitations to conferences”, says Yanlan Mao of University College London. Trying to balance the two can produce extreme travel arrangements: Yanlan once travelled from the UK for a two-day trip to China.

## Flexibility is a double-edged sword

When asked what is the biggest advantage scientist parents have over parents in other careers, there was a clear consensus: flexibility. Most researchers are free to work when they like, although this benefit does come with a number of caveats. “My partner always says that academics have the freedom to work whichever 60 hours a week they choose”, says Adrian Liston of VIB in Belgium. In addition, certain tasks are better suited to flexible working than others. Grant applications and papers can be written at home, and it is often possible to perform computational research and data analysis remotely. However, many a planned wet lab experiment or field study has been postponed because of a sick child.

And while research can be performed at almost any time of day, children often have strict schedules: the start and end of the school or nursery day, for example, are inflexible. To accommodate leaving ‘early’ to pick up children, many parents resume work once the children are in bed. That said, several researchers mentioned to us that they struggle to leave work behind completely when spending time with their children. “Block those precious times with your kids off, and then when you actually do work, you will be more efficient” is Yanlan Mao’s advice. However, some parents told us that they cannot work at the same rate and intensity as they did before they had children.

## Better for everyone

Making scientific careers more family-friendly would benefit scientists without children too. The constant pressure to perform to get the next job and the next grant is experienced by all researchers, not just those who are also parents. By making it more acceptable to work flexibly – in the same institute for your whole career, if you choose – scientific careers will become more accessible to a diverse group of researchers, particularly those with other caring responsibilities and those with disabilities and chronic conditions.

A research career should not be a barrier to having children, and vice versa. “Research is not just a job”, says Gaby Da Silva Xavier. “I would not be me if I gave up on my work, and that arguably would not make me a good role model for my son”. As we hope to show in this series, having both is achievable and can enrich the lives of researchers and the people they work with.

## Note

This Feature Article is part of the Scientist and Parent collection.

results.result: On-campus childcare is a key pressure point for scientist parents due to cost, availability, and eligibility barriers. Waiting lists are months-long, costs can exceed half a researcher's salary even with subsidies, and scholarship-funded postdocs may be ineligible for on-site facilities.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C12 provide converging evidence from multiple sources (general observations, specific anecdotes from Marta Garrido, and structural employment issues) that collectively document significant childcare barriers. The anecdotal examples (C6-C8) illustrate the severity of waiting lists, while quantitative claims (C10) and eligibility issues (C11-C12) demonstrate cost and access barriers.

results.result: There are wider disparities in benefits offered to different classes of postdoctoral researchers, leading to calls for more consistent employment contracts.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C14 are supported by citation to Schaller et al., 2017, providing external validation for the observation about postdoc employment disparities. The childcare eligibility issue (C11-C12) serves as a concrete example of these broader disparities.

results.result: Parental leave policies for researchers vary widely based on national standards and gender, with additional complications for those on fixed-term contracts. Researchers may work through leave due to professional pressures, and the collaborative nature of science creates psychological barriers to taking leave.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C23 describe multiple dimensions of parental leave challenges through general observations and reported experiences. The claims logically connect structural factors (C15-C18), behavioral responses (C19-C21), and psychological pressures (C22-C23), though they rely primarily on qualitative data without quantitative validation.

results.result: Various initiatives from employers, funders, and organizations provide support for parents returning from maternity leave, such as fellowships to employ additional lab personnel.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C25 are supported by a specific example (Gaby Da Silva Xavier's use of an Elsie Widdowson Fellowship). However, the scope and effectiveness of such initiatives are not quantified, limiting assessment of their broader impact.

results.result: Career mobility expectations and short-term contracts cause scientist parents to relocate internationally, often resulting in family separation and loss of support networks. The case of Ali Twelvetrees illustrates the emotional and financial hardship of such arrangements.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C35 combine general observations about mobility pressures with a detailed case study of Ali Twelvetrees. The specific biographical details (C30-C35) and direct quotes (C33-C34) provide concrete evidence for the emotional and financial costs of mobility-driven family separation.

results.result: Conference attendance creates difficult choices for researcher parents between family time and professional networking, despite emerging childcare support from some organizers. Extreme travel arrangements may result from attempts to balance these competing demands.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C40 document conference-related challenges through general observations and specific examples from Yanlan Mao. The extreme travel example (C40) effectively illustrates the lengths to which researchers go to balance professional and family obligations, though the prevalence of such arrangements is not quantified.

results.result: Flexibility is identified as the primary advantage for scientist parents, allowing work at various times and locations, though this comes with caveats including high total work hours, inflexible childcare schedules, and limitations for certain research types. Many parents work after children are in bed and struggle with work-life boundaries.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C54 present a nuanced view of flexibility through consensus findings (C41), specific examples (C44, C47, C51-C52), and practical advice (C53). The claims acknowledge both benefits and limitations, providing a balanced assessment supported by multiple researcher perspectives, though without quantitative data on prevalence or outcomes.

results.result: Making scientific careers more family-friendly would benefit all researchers, not just parents, by addressing universal pressures and making careers accessible to diverse groups including those with caring responsibilities, disabilities, and chronic conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C59 present logical arguments about broader benefits of family-friendly policies, but these remain largely speculative (C55, C57-C59 are marked as INFERENCE). While C56 accurately describes universal career pressures, the causal claims about improved accessibility lack empirical validation or supporting evidence.

results.result: The article concludes that research careers and parenthood should be mutually compatible, with having both being achievable and potentially enriching for researchers and their colleagues.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C65 represent normative statements (C60-C61 marked as SPECULATION) and aspirational conclusions (C64-C65). While C62-C63 provide one researcher's perspective, the broader claims about achievability and enrichment are presented as goals rather than demonstrated outcomes, lacking systematic evidence from the article series.

results.result: eLife is publishing a collection of articles and interviews exploring how scientists can successfully combine parenthood with research careers.
results.evaluation: Claim C1 is a straightforward factual statement about the article series itself, directly stated in the abstract and confirmed by the manuscript content.
